study_identification.author_journal_year: Sampaio et al., Artificial Intelligence in Medicine, 2025
study_identification.title: A generalizable normative deep autoencoder for brain morphological anomaly detection: application to the multi-site StratiBip dataset on bipolar disorder in an external validation framework

study_characteristics.study_objective: To develop and validate a generalizable deep learning-based normative modeling framework for brain morphology using autoencoders, embedded in an external validation framework with confounder removal, and apply it to characterize brain structural deviations in bipolar disorder (BD) at both group and individual levels.

preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: All sMRI data were pre-processed in Matlab R2018a (The Mathworks, Inc.®) environment. Firstly, T1-weighted images underwent a visual quality check and were converted from DICOM to NIFTI format. Following, the pre-processing was performed using the statistical parametric mapping software (SPM12) version 7771 [39], available at (http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/software/spm12/), and the computational anatomy toolbox add-on (CAT12) version 12.7 [40]. Supplementary: We used the CAT12 pre-processing modules included in the standard voxel-based morphometry (VBM) starting with spatial registration using DARTEL (Diffeomorphic Anatomical Registration Through Exponentiated Lie algebra) resulting images were normalized to a reference template brain, the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space, followed by brain tissue segmentation, bias correction of intensity non-homogeneities, spatial normalization, modulation with the Jacobian determinant derived from the previous step to preserve the total amount of signal from each region, and spatial smoothing with a 3D Gaussian kernel with full-width half maximum of 6 mm. Surface-based morphometry was also performed to estimate cortical thickness using the projection-based thickness method.

site_effect_handling.reason: The paper explicitly describes using ComBat harmonization for site effect removal, which is a batch-removal technique.
site_effect_handling.supporting_text: To address this, we developed a pipeline to harmonize brain features from the multi-site StratiBip external test set with the HCP-YA training set. This step was aimed to remove both intratest set and inter-dataset differences, enabling the reliable application of the trained AE normative model in an EV framework. The pipeline was based on the ComBat (Combatting Batch Effects) tool, described below.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Modified ComBat (M-ComBat) harmonization was used to remove site effects. The model was fitted exclusively on the normative HCP-YA sample concatenated with the healthy control portion of the StratiBip test set (N=363 HC), and then applied to all test data (both HC and BD). Site was treated as the batch variable. Biological covariates (age, sex, and harmonized TIV for volumes) were preserved during harmonization using linear regression. The harmonization pipeline standardized data using HCP-YA statistics, estimated additive (gamma) and multiplicative (delta) site effects using Empirical Bayes framework, and then removed these effects. Efficacy was evaluated through: 1) Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA comparing feature distributions across sites before/after harmonization; 2) UMAP projections showing cluster reduction; 3) SVM site classification showing decreased performance (f1-score from 95% to 23%) after harmonization; 4) Preservation of biological covariate associations before/after harmonization (Spearman correlations >0.96).
site_effect_handling_detail.reason: The paper provides extensive detail about the M-ComBat harmonization method in both main text and supplementary materials, including mathematical formulations, validation approaches, and efficacy metrics.
site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: Harmonization pipeline. We propose an innovative pipeline to enable site harmonization of non-normative external datasets with the normative training set, as shown in Fig. 2. In this case, the M-ComBat model was fitted exclusively on a normative sample and later applied to all test data. First, the external test set (StratiBip) HC portion (N = 363), yij = HC, v, is concatenated with the HCP-YA normative training set, which was used as the reference i = HCP to estimate the StratiBip site-effects. Also: We checked the quality of site effect removal performed via MComBat application. Before harmonization, all feature set distributions (GMV, WMV, CT) for the HCs among the 8 sites (HCP site and 7 StratiBip sites) resulted significantly different (p < 1e-29) but no differences were detected among sites after harmonization (p > 0.680). Also supplementary: We computed the Spearman correlation between biocovariates beta coefficients, β, pre and post-harmonization, from the intra-site LR models. All the correlations resulted statistically significant (p<10-22) with r coefficients > 0.96.

modeling_method.supporting_text: Deep learning (DL) autoencoder (AE) models have been widely employed in anomaly detection frameworks and have emerged as suitable multivariate models for brain normative frameworks [23-25]. These models, which are based on artificial neural networks, have an encoder-decoder architecture designed to capture relevant regularities in data through the minimization of the input reconstruction error (RE). Also in title: A generalizable normative deep autoencoder for brain morphological anomaly detection

predictor_variables.supporting_text: After data harmonization, we proceeded with the removal of variance associated with age and sex biocovariates from regional volumes and CT features, and harmonized TIV from volume features, via standard LR [51,52]. predictor_effects.answer: In the confounder removal pipeline: Age and Sex modeled as fixed effects in linear regression (effects removed from data); TIV modeled as fixed effect for volumes (effects removed); Site modeled with empirical Bayes framework in ComBat (additive gamma and multiplicative delta site effects estimated and removed). The autoencoder itself is unsupervised and does not model predictor effects explicitly.
predictor_effects.reason: The paper clearly describes how biological covariates (age, sex, TIV) were modeled as fixed effects in linear regression and removed, while site effects were modeled using empirical Bayes in ComBat harmonization.
predictor_effects.supporting_text: We considered the outlined biological covariates as confounding variables as these are implicitly encoded in neuroimaging data and would contribute to a source ambiguity problem of the later developed AE model. We embedded the LR estimations and corrections in the EV, consistently with the proposed CR pipeline. The LR coefficient estimations were performed exclusively on the HCP-YA training set, and the estimated effects were removed from both HCP-YA training set and StratiBip test set [53,54]. Supplementary: ComBat models biological covariates, such as age, sex, a priori, with a linear regression.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.answer: Yes, nuisance structure was appropriately handled through a comprehensive confounder removal pipeline before normative modeling. Site effects (mean shifts, variance differences across sites) were removed using Modified ComBat harmonization with empirical Bayes estimation of additive and multiplicative site effects. Biological covariates (age, sex, TIV) were removed via linear regression. Validation of nuisance structure handling included: 1) Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA showing no significant site differences after harmonization (p>0.68 for HC); 2) SVM site classification performance dropping from 95% to 23% f1-score after harmonization; 3) UMAP projections showing elimination of site-based clustering; 4) Preservation of biological covariate effects with Spearman correlations >0.96 between pre- and post-harmonization beta coefficients.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The paper provides extensive evidence of appropriately handling multiple forms of nuisance structure (site effects, age, sex, TIV) through ComBat harmonization and linear regression, with thorough validation of the effectiveness of these methods.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: To address this, we developed a pipeline to harmonize brain features from the multi-site StratiBip external test set with the HCP-YA training set. This step was aimed to remove both intratest set and inter-dataset differences, enabling the reliable application of the trained AE normative model in an EV framework. Also: We checked the quality of site effect removal performed via MComBat application. Before harmonization, all feature set distributions (GMV, WMV, CT) for the HCs among the 8 sites (HCP site and 7 StratiBip sites) resulted significantly different (p < 1e-29) but no differences were detected among sites after harmonization (p > 0.680). Also: A substantial decline in average f1-score was observed in the validation portion (N = 836), from 95% before harmonization to 23% after harmonization

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.answer: Yes, the normative model was validated using non-independent data from the same HCP-YA training dataset through Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOO-CV). In each fold, all subjects except one were used to train the normative AE model, and the left-out subject was used as test sample to extract reconstructions. This LOO-CV analysis was performed to extract unbiased reconstructions for all HCP-YA training set subjects and to construct normative RE distributions for each feature used for subject-level inference. A 10-fold cross-validation was also performed during hyperparameter tuning.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The paper explicitly describes using LOO-CV on the HCP-YA training set to obtain unbiased reconstructions for validation purposes, and 10-fold CV for hyperparameter tuning.

Also: The number of layers, the number of neurons, the batch size, the number of epochs, the learning rate and the l2 norm coefficient were optimized in a 10 fold CV hyperparameter tunning process with a random search strategy

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.answer: Yes, the normative model was validated using a different domain dataset - the multi-site StratiBip network comprising 550 subjects (363 HC and 187 BD) from 7 different sites. This external validation framework involved: 1) Harmonization of the StratiBip test set with HCP-YA training set using M-ComBat; 2) Removal of biological covariate effects using coefficients estimated from HCP-YA; 3) Application of the trained AE model to extract reconstruction errors (REs) and mean deviation scores (MDS); 4) Group-level analysis showing BD group had significantly higher MDS (median 0.2264 vs 0.1988 for HC, non-overlapping 95% CIs); 5) ROC analysis achieving AUC of 0.6129 for HC vs BD discrimination; 6) Feature-level analysis identifying significant deviations in specific brain regions; 7) Subject-level abnormality detection using modified z-scores. The model achieved training loss MSE of 0.182 and validation loss MSE of 0.222 on the external set. Bootstrap validation (1000 iterations) was used to assess model robustness.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The paper extensively describes external validation on the StratiBip dataset, which differs from HCP-YA in multiple domains: different cohort/consortium, multiple sites (7 vs 1), different scanners and acquisition protocols, different age distribution (StratiBip-HC younger than HCP-YA, p=1.73e-6), and inclusion of clinical population (BD patients).
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: An innovative end-to-end pipeline was designed to manage both biological and site-related confounding sources, embedded in an external validation (EV) framework [27]. The normative model framework was trained on the confounders-free brain features extracted from the human connectome project young adults (HCP-YA) dataset [28] and applied to multi-site data from the StratiBip network [16], including HC and subjects with BD. Also: The external test set consisted of data collected as part of the StratiBip network, an initiative that originated from the ENPACT network [16]. The StratiBip dataset results from the post-hoc integration of multi-site clinical and neuroimaging data collected from HC and subjects with BD Also: When trained on the HCP-YA training set, the AE normative model achieved a training loss MSE of 0.182 ([0.179;0.185]; 95% CI) and a validation loss MSE of 0.222 ([0.211;0.233]; 95% CI)

deviation_metric.answer: Primary: Mean Deviation Score (MDS) - average squared reconstruction error across all 170 features. Secondary: Reconstruction Error (RE) per feature - squared error between original and reconstructed values. Individual-level: Modified z-scores (mZ) using median and median absolute deviation (MAD) from normative HCP-YA distribution, with feature-specific 99th percentile thresholds for abnormality detection. Extreme values: Mean of Extreme Values (MEV) - 99% trimmed mean (top 1% of values).

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Group-level comparisons: Bootstrap analysis (1000 iterations) comparing feature-wise MDS between BD and HC groups, with Cliff's delta effect size and uncorrected p<0.05 threshold. ROC curve analysis using subject-level MDS to discriminate BD vs HC, reporting AUC-ROC with 95% CI. Comparison of Mean of Extreme Values (MEV) between BD, HC, and HCP-YA groups using 99% trimmed mean. Individual-level analysis: Modified z-scores (mZ) calculated for each subject and feature, with abnormality defined as exceeding the feature-specific 99th percentile threshold from normative HCP-YA distribution. Spatial overlap analysis calculating proportion of BD subjects showing abnormalities in each brain region. Comparison with mass-univariate analysis using two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: The autoencoder-based normative model successfully detected significantly higher brain morphological deviations in BD patients compared to healthy controls (MDS median 0.2264 vs 0.1988, non-overlapping 95% CIs), with BD-specific abnormalities in limbic and cerebellar regions, demonstrating heterogeneity at the individual level but limited discriminative power at the group level (AUC-ROC 0.6129).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The AE normative model trained on 1109 HCP-YA subjects (training MSE 0.182, validation MSE 0.222) identified significantly higher deviations in BD patients versus healthy controls, with median MDS of 0.2264 [0.2210, 0.2324; 95% CI] for BD compared to 0.1988 [0.1945, 0.2030; 95% CI] for HC (median difference -0.02760 [-0.03390, -0.02155; 95% CI]). ROC analysis for BD vs HC discrimination yielded AUC-ROC 0.6129 [0.5989, 0.6270] with optimal threshold 0.2138, achieving 58.3% accuracy. Feature-level analysis (bootstrap with Cliff's delta, p<0.05 uncorrected) identified higher BD deviations in: cortical thickness of right inferior temporal gyrus; gray matter volumes in cerebellum and limbic structures (hippocampus, striatum, globus pallidus); and white matter volumes adjacent to these subcortical regions. Extreme value analysis (MEV using 99% trimmed mean) showed BD group had 7 CT, 4 GMV, and 4 WMV features with at least double the MEV compared to both normative HCP-YA and StratiBip-HC groups; using MEV improved discrimination to AUC-ROC 0.6218 [0.5999, 0.6452] with 59.0% accuracy. Individual-level analysis using modified z-scores with feature-specific 99th percentile thresholds showed heterogeneity in deviation patterns: only 21 of 187 BD subjects (11.2%) exceeded abnormality threshold in ≥50% of features. Spatial overlap analysis revealed that no single brain region was abnormal in more than 50% of BD patients, with highest overlap (~27%) in bilateral globus pallidus white matter. Comparison with mass-univariate analysis (Mann-Whitney U test) showed limited overlap (overlap coefficient 0.14); only left globus pallidus white matter survived FDR correction in univariate analysis. Bootstrap validation (1000 iterations) demonstrated model robustness. The confounder removal pipeline successfully eliminated site effects (f1-score for site classification dropped from 95% to 23% after harmonization; p>0.68 for post-harmonization site differences) while preserving biological covariate effects (Spearman correlations >0.96).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Key limitations include: 1) Lack of external clinical validation set to evaluate false positive rates and clinical applicability; 2) Use of ROI-level rather than voxel-level analysis, which reduced granularity but avoided overfitting and dimensionality issues; 3) Moderate discriminative performance (AUC ~0.61-0.62) limiting immediate clinical application; 4) Uncertainty in CAT12 tissue segmentation, particularly for subcortical regions with reduced GM-WM contrast due to iron content; 5) Post-hoc integration of multi-site data with heterogeneous acquisition protocols; 6) Age range limited to young adults (22-37 years), restricting generalizability across lifespan; 7) Lack of detailed clinical characterization and symptom severity correlations; 8) BD heterogeneity not fully characterized (BD-I vs BD-II subtypes, mood states, medication effects not analyzed); 9) Small sample sizes at some individual sites (Site 1: N=3 BD; Site 4: N=6 BD); 10) Potential biases in tissue probability estimation for mixed-tissue regions.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The framework demonstrates proof-of-concept for generalizable deep learning normative modeling with comprehensive confounder control in external validation settings. Authors emphasize the heterogeneity of BD at individual level, with personalized deviation maps showing diverse patterns across patients. The moderate group-level discrimination suggests limited immediate clinical utility for diagnosis but potential for: 1) Stratifying BD subgroups with marked deviations; 2) Identifying individuals with extreme values in specific brain regions; 3) Future integration with symptom severity measures and clinical outcomes; 4) Extension to other psychiatric disorders in transdiagnostic frameworks; 5) Application to voxel-level data with appropriate model adaptations. The Modified ComBat harmonization pipeline enabling normative site effect correction in external datasets is a notable methodological contribution. The study highlights the importance of moving from categorical diagnoses to dimensional, patient-centered approaches capturing individual heterogeneity.

general_notes.general_notes: BD subtypes included: The sample included both BD-I and BD-II subtypes across sites with BD-I representing majority in most sites. BD age of onset reported for most sites (mean range 18.15-24.42 years). Scanner/acquisition heterogeneity: 7 different sites with varying scanners (Siemens Allegra, Philips Achieva 3T, Siemens Tim Trio, Philips Intera) and different sequences (T1-MPRAGE, 3D-MPRAGE, TFE, FFE). Final autoencoder architecture: Input 170 features, single hidden layer with 100 neurons, latent dimension 60, learning rate 0.00005, batch size 32, epochs 2000, L2 regularizer 0.0005, selu activation (hidden), linear activation (output). Code availability: GitHub (https://github.com/inesws/Normative_AE) and neuro-combat_pyClasse for harmonization. Ethical approval obtained at all sites following Declaration of Helsinki. Diagnosis based on SCID-I (DSM-IV) for all sites except Vancouver (MINI). Exclusion criteria included comorbidities, intellectual disability, pregnancy, epilepsy history, major medical/neurological disorders, neuroleptic treatment in last 3 months, drug/alcohol abuse in last 6 months. Novel contribution: First study demonstrating effective mitigation of site-related and biological confounding effects in DL analysis pipeline in external validation framework using M-ComBat approach.
